leads.title: Oracle against Moab: wine settled on its lees, Chemosh into exile ↔ Oracles against Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar and Hazor, and Elam
leads.summary: 5 shared motifs, found by the separate reads; not yet compared side by side.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: The enemy swoops like an eagle and spreads its wings over a land (weight 6.7); The heart of warriors on that day is like the heart of a woman in labor (weight 6.7); A conquered nation's god goes into exile with his priests and princes (weight 6.7); God will restore the fortunes of a foreign nation in the latter days (weight 6.7); Brief oracles against neighboring nations (Amalek, Kenite, Asshur, Kittim) (weight 4.6). Pair score 31.4.

Only in Oracle against Moab: wine settled on its lees, Chemosh into exile: Lament: how the mighty staff, the glorious rod, is broken; The nation is broken like a vessel no one wants; Long list of Moabite towns under judgment (Dibon, Nebo, Kiriathaim, Kerioth, Bozrah...); Cursed is he who does YHWH's work slackly and keeps his sword from blood; Refugees told to dwell in the rocks like a dove nesting in the sides of a gorge; 'Give wings to Moab', for she must flee away; The joyful 'hedad' shout of grape-treaders falls silent; Fugitives become like a juniper (or wild ass) in the desert; A nation made drunk wallows in its vomit and becomes a laughing-stock; The great pride, arrogance and haughtiness of Moab; The vine of Sibmah whose tendrils crossed the sea, now despoiled; A nation at ease like wine settled on its lees, never poured from vessel to vessel; and 6 more.

Only in Oracles against Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar and Hazor, and Elam: Desert peoples described as those with the corners of their hair clipped; God breaks the bow of Elam, the chief of their might; A people at ease that dwells alone with neither gates nor bars; The cry at a nation's fall is heard as far as the Red Sea; God brings the four winds from the four ends of heaven to scatter a people; God sets his own throne in a conquered foreign land; Milcom (their 'king') dispossessed the tribe of Gad and will go into exile; Though you make your nest as high as the eagle's, God will bring you down; Fire kindled in the wall of Damascus devours the palaces of Ben-hadad; A ruined city becomes a haunt of jackals, desolate forever; An envoy is sent among the nations to summon them to battle; Grape-gatherers would leave gleanings and thieves take only enough, but God strips the nation bare; and 7 more.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: God permits the adversary to afflict a righteous man, within set limits, to test his loyalty (weight 6.7); God points out his servant as unmatched on earth for piety (weight 6.7); The sons of God present themselves before YHWH in a heavenly assembly (weight 6.7); A heavenly being reports he has been roaming to and fro on the earth (weight 6.0); The Satan (the adversary) appears in the heavenly court as an accusing member (weight 6.0); Men tear their garments in grief or dismay (weight 4.9). Pair score 37.0.

Only in Job's piety, the heavenly council and the first test: The verb 'bless' (barekh) used as a scribal euphemism for cursing God; Grown sons hold feasts in turn, each on his day, and invite their sisters; A great wind from the desert strikes the four corners of the house and it falls on the feasting children; God has set a protective hedge around the righteous man, his house and goods; 'Fire of God' falls from heaven and consumes flocks and servants; Messenger after messenger arrives while the last is still speaking, each the sole survivor of a disaster; 'I alone escaped to tell you'; 'Does he fear God for nothing?': piety suspected of being motivated by reward; The exemplary righteous man is a non-Israelite living in the land of Uz in the east; Father offers burnt offerings in case his children 'blessed' (cursed) God in their hearts; A blessed man has seven sons and three daughters; Mourner shaves his head and falls to the ground; and 15 more.

Only in The second test; Job's wife; the three friends: 'Shall we accept the good from God and not accept the evil?'; The sufferer is struck with sore boils from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head; Mourners throw dust on their heads toward the sky; The sufferer sits among the ashes scraping himself with a potsherd; Comforters sit on the ground with the sufferer seven days and nights without speaking; Adversary's proverb 'skin for skin': a man gives all he has for his life; Friends see the sufferer from afar and do not recognize him; Three friends from distant places arrange to come together to console the sufferer; The sufferer's wife urges him 'Curse God and die'; How a worshipper responds to good fortune and to misfortune sent by God [contrast between the texts]; Seven days of mourning for the dead.

leads.title: YHWH sayings and royal sayings (man plans, God disposes) ↔ Sayings on wine, the king's throne and the lamp of YHWH
leads.summary: 6 shared motifs, found by the separate reads; not yet compared side by side.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Grey hair is a crown of glory, found in the way of righteousness (weight 6.7); The throne is established by righteousness (and loyalty) (weight 6.0); Getting wisdom is better than gold, understanding than silver or jewels (weight 6.0); The heart of man plans his way but YHWH directs his steps; only YHWH's counsel stands (weight 5.8); Saying of the type 'X is an abomination (to'evah) to YHWH but Y is his delight' (weight 5.6); Honest balances, weights, ephah and hin are commanded (weight 4.7). Pair score 34.8.

Only in YHWH sayings and royal sayings (man plans, God disposes): By loyalty and faithfulness (hesed we-emet) iniquity is atoned for; When a man's ways please YHWH he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him; YHWH has made everything for its purpose, even the wicked for the day of evil; The worker's appetite works for him, for his mouth urges him on; In the light of the king's face is life; his favor is like a cloud of the latter rain; The wrath of a king is messengers of death, but a wise man will pacify it; The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from YHWH; Divination (qesem) is on the lips of the king; his mouth does not err in judgment; Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the bones; Roll (commit) your works to YHWH and your plans will be established; The worthless man (ish beliyya'al) digs up evil and on his lips is a scorching fire; A whisperer separates close friends; and 8 more.

Only in Sayings on wine, the king's throne and the lamp of YHWH: Bruising wounds scour away evil; blows cleanse the inner chambers; Bread gained by deceit is sweet, but afterwards the mouth is filled with gravel; 'Bad, bad,' says the buyer, then goes away and boasts; Counsel in a man's heart is deep water; a man of understanding draws it out; He who curses father or mother, his lamp is put out in the pupil of darkness; Many proclaim their loyalty, but a faithful man who can find?; The breath (nishmat) of man is the lamp of YHWH, searching all the inner chambers of the belly; A king seated on the throne of judgment winnows all evil with his eyes; A wise king winnows the wicked and drives the threshing wheel over them; It is a snare to say rashly 'Holy!' and only afterwards to reflect on vows; The sluggard does not plow in autumn; he asks at harvest and has nothing; The glory of young men is their strength, the splendor of the old their grey hair; and 14 more.

leads.title: Psalm 78, Asaph's historical recital from Egypt to David ↔ Psalm 105, historical hymn from the patriarchs through Joseph and the exodus
leads.summary: 14 shared motifs, found by the separate reads; not yet compared side by side.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Swarms (arov) of insects or wild beasts fill the houses of Egypt (weight 6.3); Moses was given nine clear signs [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.3); Egypt is called 'the tents of Ham' or 'the land of Ham' (weight 6.3); A poetic list of the Egyptian plagues differs in number and order from Exodus (weight 6.0); Frogs swarm out of the river into houses, beds, ovens and kneading-troughs (weight 6.0); Water brought out of a rock by the leader's rod (weight 6.0); God kills every firstborn of the land, from the king's heir to the lowest servant and cattle (weight 6.0); God rains bread from heaven to feed the people in the desert (weight 6.0); Quail come up in the evening and cover the camp (weight 6.0); God sends hail mingled with fire and thunder from heaven (weight 5.8); Nile water is turned to blood (weight 5.8); Psalm retells Israel's sacred history (patriarchs, Egypt, wilderness, conquest) as instruction or praise (weight 5.6); Locusts brought by an east wind devour all vegetation left after the hail (weight 5.6); God leads the people in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night (weight 5.1). Pair score 82.6.

Only in Psalm 78, Asaph's historical recital from Egypt to David: God sends a band (mishlahat) of 'evil angels' (mal'akhei ra'im) to execute his wrath; Manna called 'bread of the mighty ones' (lehem abbirim), i.e. food of angels; God struck his enemies backward/in the rear (read by rabbis as the Philistines' hemorrhoids); The exodus wonders are located in 'the field of Zoan' (Tanis); The Lord awakes as from sleep like a warrior shouting from wine; God remembers that humans are flesh, a breath that passes and does not return; God rejected the tent of Joseph and tribe of Ephraim and chose Judah and Mount Zion; In the catastrophe young men are consumed by fire, maidens have no wedding song, widows do not lament; God built his sanctuary like the heights (or heavens) and like the earth founded forever; God took David from the sheepfolds, from following the nursing ewes, to shepherd his people; The ark of God is captured by enemies; God commanded the skies and opened the doors (or windows) of heaven; and 27 more.

Only in Psalm 105, historical hymn from the patriarchs through Joseph and the exodus: Egypt rejoiced when Israel left, for dread of them had fallen on it; God turned the Egyptians' hearts to hate his people and deal craftily with them; Joseph's feet were hurt in fetters and his neck (nefesh) put in iron until his word came true; God sent a man ahead of them: Joseph, sold as a slave; Joseph was to bind the king's princes at will and teach his elders wisdom; At the exodus not one among the tribes stumbled (or was feeble); God calls the patriarchs his 'anointed ones' and 'prophets' and rebukes kings for their sake ('Touch not my anointed'); God opened the rock and waters gushed and ran as a river in the desert; The ancestors were few in number, sojourners wandering from nation to nation; The chain of patriarchs to whom revelation or covenant passed [divergence between the texts]; The number of signs or plagues in Egypt [divergence between the texts]; A palpable darkness covers the land for three days; and 19 more.

וַיִּ֜מַח אֶֽת כָּל הַיְק֣וּם אֲשֶׁ֣ר עַל פְּנֵ֣י הָֽאֲדָמָ֗ה מֵאָדָ֤ם עַד בְּהֵמָה֙ עַד רֶ֨מֶשׂ֙ וְעַד ע֣וֹף הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וַיִּמָּח֖וּ מִן הָאָ֑רֶץ וַיִשָּׁ֧אֶר אַךְ נֹ֛חַ וַֽאֲשֶׁ֥ר אִתּ֖וֹ בַּתֵּבָֽה

leads.title: Dara Shikoh's Upanishads reach Schopenhauer
leads.summary: Dara Shikoh translated 50 Upanishads into Persian as the Sirr-i Akbar (1657). Anquetil-Duperron's Latin version (Oupnek'hat, 1801–02) is how Schopenhauer read them.

passages.ref: Dara Shikoh, Sirr-i Akbar (1657); Majmaʿ al-Baḥrayn (1655)

evidence.text: Majmaʿ al-Baḥrayn ('the meeting of the two seas') takes its title from Quran 18:60.

leads.title: Plotinus as the 'Theology of Aristotle'
leads.summary: An Arabic paraphrase of Plotinus' Enneads IV–VI circulated as the 'Theology of Aristotle' (al-Kindi's circle, 9th c.) and shaped Islamic Neoplatonism.

leads.title: Ancient treaty form and Deuteronomy's covenant
leads.summary: Deuteronomy follows the structure of ancient Near Eastern vassal treaties: preamble, history, stipulations, deposit, witnesses, curses and blessings.

evidence.text: Mendenhall (1954) argued for the Hittite model. Many scholars now consider Neo-Assyrian treaties the closer parallel. Which source is closer is the open question.
